detroit.heading: Community gardening in Detroit: where to start
paragraphs: Detroit does not appear to have one citywide plot waitlist. The main support network is Keep Growing Detroit, a nonprofit whose Garden Resource Program is open to gardens in Detroit, Highland Park and Hamtramck. Gardeners join by completing an online or PDF application, and memberships run by calendar year, so past members reapply each year.

The program has separate membership types for family gardens and for community, school or market gardens, and it offers a fee waiver or reduction option on the application. Fees can change, so check the page. Keep Growing Detroit also says it can help you think through where to start a garden, so it is a sensible first contact if you want land rather than a ready-made plot.

links.label: Keep Growing Detroit: Garden Resource Program

seattle.heading: How to get a P-Patch plot in Seattle
paragraphs: Seattle's public community gardens are the P-Patches, run by the city's Department of Neighborhoods. You join an interest list rather than reserving a plot directly. You must live in the City of Seattle (the city notes limited exceptions), and you can be on two garden lists at a time. Lists are ordered by date of first request, and the city checks in with people each fall to confirm they are still interested.

Wait times vary a lot by garden. Individual garden pages on the city's site list waits from about 6 to 12 months at some gardens and 1 to 2 years at others, so pick gardens near you and check the current figure on each garden's page.

links.label: Seattle P-Patch: how to sign up

ottawa-gatineau.heading: Community gardens in Ottawa: how the City program works
paragraphs: This section describes the City of Ottawa side of the region, not Gatineau. Ottawa's Community-led Greening Initiatives and Gardening Program, run by Recreation, Cultural and Facility Services, helps groups start or maintain gardens on City-owned land. Eligible applicants are not-for-profit groups, incorporated or not, such as community associations and resident-led groups. Applications go through a single review process.

Individual plots are not assigned through that application. The City's page does not cover waitlists or plot assignment, and points to ottawa.ca/gardens or communitygardens@ottawa.ca for those questions. Intake windows have been announced by season, so check the page for the current one, since this can change. In practice, residents join an existing garden group or form one.

links.label: City of Ottawa: community gardens and greening FAQ

philadelphia.heading: How to find a community garden plot in Philadelphia
paragraphs: Philadelphia has no single sign-up for community garden plots. Neighborhood Gardens Trust, a nonprofit that preserves community gardens, publishes a garden map. You find gardens near you, open a pin for details and the best contact person, and ask that garden about joining.

Each garden handles its own membership, and the Trust notes that many have waitlists because demand for plots is high. If the map does not lead you to a contact, the Trust lists an email address and phone number on its site. Gardens outside the Trust's network have their own processes.

chicago.heading: Community gardens in Chicago: who runs them
paragraphs: Chicago community gardens mostly sit on one of two kinds of land. The Chicago Park District's Community Gardens in the Parks program supports garden groups on park land, and its page lists more than 90 gardens. NeighborSpace is a nonprofit land trust that holds title to community gardens on other city lots so neighborhood groups can manage them.

Which one applies depends on where a garden is, so start by finding the garden near you on the map and then contact the program that covers its land. The Park District publishes forms for new garden groups and expansions, and NeighborSpace asks for an organizational partner and a team of garden leaders before it takes on a site.

toronto.heading: How to join or start a community garden in Toronto
paragraphs: On Toronto's community garden page, the City says gardens are managed by community members or agencies. To join one, you pick a garden from the City's list by district and contact the City's community gardens program supervisor; some gardens keep waiting lists.

To start a garden, the City asks for a group of at least five residents plus one or two leaders to liaise with staff, on a City-owned park site. Staff review the site before you write a proposal. After a proposal is submitted, the local councillor's office runs a community consultation, and gardening cannot begin until the City approves. Contact details on the page can change, so check it.

montreal.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Montréal
paragraphs: In Montréal, community gardens are handled borough by borough. Some are run by the borough's own recreation department, and others by partner groups such as horticultural societies or éco-quartiers. You join a waiting list for a garden in your borough, residents generally get priority, and plots are usually given out in order of registration.

The City's page says waits often exceed a year and that registering does not guarantee a plot this year or next. It lists typical requirements such as photo ID and proof of address, and some boroughs ask for a citizen or library card. Costs vary by borough, so check the page for yours. The City's page is in French.

links.label: Ville de Montréal: obtenir un espace dans un jardin communautaire (French)

vancouver.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Vancouver
paragraphs: The City of Vancouver lists its community gardens on a map, with each garden's organizer and contact details. According to the City, many gardens have waitlists for plots, and those waitlists are managed by each garden rather than by the City.

That means there is no single application. Choose a few gardens near you from the map, contact each organizer, and ask how to get on the list and whether membership has requirements. Details differ from garden to garden, so check the City's page and the garden itself for current information.

links.label: City of Vancouver: community gardens and orchards

boston.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Boston
paragraphs: Boston has no central sign-up for garden plots. The city's Community Garden and Urban Farm Directory, from GrowBoston, lists each garden with a contact, and you apply through that contact. Gardens are run by different groups, including Boston Parks and Recreation, The Trustees, Southwest Corridor Park and neighborhood nonprofits.

Waitlists vary a lot, from none at some gardens to several years at others, and the directory notes that its figures can be dated. A few gardens limit plots to residents of certain neighborhoods or buildings, and some food forests have no individual plots at all. Fees also vary and can change, so confirm with the garden before you apply.

links.label: GrowBoston: community garden and urban farm directory

baltimore.heading: Community gardens in Baltimore: starting one on a vacant lot
paragraphs: The City of Baltimore's sustainability office page does not describe how to rent a plot in an existing garden. It focuses on starting green space. Its Adopt-A-Lot option, run by the Department of Housing and Community Development through Vacants to Value, lets residents adopt city-owned vacant lots in their neighborhood for community green space.

The same page also describes a Side Yard program for neighbors who want to buy an adjacent city-owned lot, and it points to Baltimore Green Space, a nonprofit that works with community groups to preserve and support community-managed gardens. Terms and prices can change, so check the page, or contact the Office of Sustainability with questions.

links.label: Baltimore Office of Sustainability: community gardens and green space

milwaukee.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Milwaukee
paragraphs: In Milwaukee, the main plot program is run by Extension Milwaukee County, part of the University of Wisconsin-Madison Division of Extension, which operates eight community gardens across the county. You request a plot with a form: online, by email to the garden rentals address, or by mail to the West Allis office. Visits are by appointment only, so email first.

Extension offers seasonal plots, which it tills for you, and year-round plots, which it does not. Its page says year-round plots have eligibility limits and long waitlists, and first-time gardeners asking for one meet with staff first. Prices and renewal dates are listed on the page, so check the page, this can change. Churches and neighborhood groups may run their own gardens with separate sign-ups.

links.label: Extension Milwaukee County: community garden rental

portland.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Portland
paragraphs: Portland Parks & Recreation runs the city's community gardens. You request a plot by reading the registration information and garden policies, then submitting one Garden Plot Request Form. Submitting it puts you on the waitlist for the garden or gardens you chose. You get no automatic confirmation, and sending duplicate forms can affect your place in line.

You can be on up to two garden waitlists at a time. The city says several gardens have waits of at least two years and most others at least one year, and plots are assigned each year from February to June as space allows. Each January the city asks people on the list to confirm they are still interested. The page does not cover residency rules or fees, so check the page or contact the Community Gardens office.

links.label: Portland Parks: request a garden plot

st-louis.heading: Finding a community garden in St. Louis
paragraphs: Seed St. Louis, the nonprofit formerly known as Gateway Greening, supports a network of community gardens, school gardens and urban orchards across the St. Louis region. Its site has a map of the network, which is the place to start if you want to find a garden or orchard near you to join.

The page does not spell out a single plot application, so how you sign up depends on the garden you pick. Seed St. Louis also has a guide for people who want to start, join or expand a garden, and its office can be reached by phone. Check its pages for current classes and contacts, since these can change.

links.label: Start, join, or expand a garden or orchard

minneapolis-st-paul.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Minneapolis
paragraphs: This section describes the Minneapolis Park and Recreation Board's program only. Saint Paul runs things differently, and plots there are usually handled garden by garden. You apply online through the park board's community garden plot application, which is also offered in Spanish, Hmong and Somali. Plots are assigned for one year at a time, you reapply each year, and each household is limited to one plot.

Anyone can apply, but Minneapolis residents get preference, along with people connected to the park, people growing food, and people with no other land to garden on. The page lists plots as free. It gives two different application deadlines, so check the page or contact the garden coordinator, this can change. Waitlists clear on September 1.

charlotte.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Charlotte
paragraphs: Most public community gardens in the Charlotte area are run by Mecklenburg County Park and Recreation, not by the City of Charlotte. You request a plot through the county's online plot request form, and the county contacts you when one opens at the garden you chose.

Demand is high, so expect to wait. The county's garden page has said plot requests can be closed for stretches because of demand, so check it for current status before you plan your season. Churches and neighborhood groups also run their own gardens, and those have their own sign-up rules.

kansas-city.heading: How to rent a community garden plot in Kansas City
paragraphs: Kansas City Community Gardens (KCCG) is a membership nonprofit that helps home gardeners grow food in backyards, vacant lots and community gardens. It has a Rent A Plot program with eight locations across the Kansas City metro, where you can rent a raised bed or a ground plot.

The pages do not explain the application steps, waitlists or who is eligible, so start with KCCG's Rent A Plot page or call its office, which is open on weekdays. Annual KCCG membership is priced on a sliding scale by household income. Check the page for current details, this can change. Some neighborhood gardens run their own separate sign-ups.

links.label: Kansas City Community Gardens: individual and family gardening

winnipeg.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Winnipeg
paragraphs: The City of Winnipeg rents individual allotment garden plots for an annual fee. Some plots are tilled once a year by the city and others are left as is, and the city does not supply water at the allotments. At the time of our last check, every city plot was listed as full for the 2026 season. To join a waiting list or ask questions, you email the Community Gardens address or call the Community Gardens phoneline.

Community gardens are a different thing. They are run by community groups, not the city, and the group handles membership, maintenance and programming under a lease with the city. So for a community garden, contact the group that runs it. The city's page also links a rental terms PDF; check the page for current fees and rules, this can change.

links.label: City of Winnipeg: allotment and community gardens

quebec-city.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Quebec City
paragraphs: The Ville de Québec uses a single waiting list for all of its municipal gardens (jardins municipaux). You must live in the city of Québec, and only one registration is allowed per civic address.
The city's page is in French. For registration questions, the city directs residents to 311.

washington.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Washington, DC
paragraphs: In Washington, DC, many community gardens are on land managed by the Department of Parks and Recreation (DPR). To get a plot, find the nearest garden on DPR's map, open it to see the garden manager's contact details, and email the manager to ask for a spot on the waiting list. If you hear nothing in a week, DPR suggests a follow-up that copies its community garden specialists.

You must be a DC resident, and each household can have only one plot. Each garden has a volunteer manager who keeps the waitlist and assigns plots. Gardeners sign a DPR waiver and code of conduct, follow garden rules, and may owe volunteer time or annual dues if their garden charges them. Other gardens, such as ones on federal land, run their own sign-ups.

denver.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Denver
paragraphs: Many community gardens in the Denver area are supported by Denver Urban Gardens (DUG), a nonprofit. Each garden is run day to day by volunteer garden leaders or a steering committee, who also handle sign-ups for new gardeners. Start by finding a garden near you in DUG's garden directory, then contact that garden's leader to ask about open plots.

Plot applications are handed out by garden leaders in spring and are not posted online, so you need to talk to a leader first. DUG's FAQ describes typical fees and plot sizes, and says fees can be waived or swapped for work, but these vary by garden and can change, so check the page. School-based gardens on Denver Public Schools property require a background check.

austin.heading: How to join or start a community garden in Austin
paragraphs: The City of Austin does not hand out plots in one central system. Its Parks and Recreation page says that to join a community garden, you contact the garden directly, and it points to the Coalition of Austin Community Gardens for contact details. Each garden decides how it handles open plots and waitlists.

If you want to start a new garden on parkland, the city's Community Gardens Program works with groups through an application and permit process. Permits apply to gardens on city-owned land, not private land. For general questions, the program lists communitygardens@austintexas.gov.

links.label: Austin: apply to start a community garden

los-angeles.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Los Angeles
paragraphs: The Los Angeles Community Garden Council is a nonprofit that works with community gardens in the Los Angeles area. There is no single sign-up list. Its site says to find a community garden near you and contact that garden's manager to request a plot.

The council also warns that a garden near you may have a waitlist before a plot opens up. Because each garden manages its own list, it can be worth contacting more than one garden. The council offers a monthly email with news on new gardens, classes and volunteer chances.

calgary.heading: Community gardens in Calgary: starting one
paragraphs: The City of Calgary's community gardens page is about starting a new garden on public land, not about assigning plots to individuals. It says to contact your local community association to find interested neighbours and choose possible sites, then submit the request through 311.

If Parks approves a location, the group meets listed requirements and submits documentation. The city says it takes applications year-round, reviews each site individually, and may offer in-kind support to new gardens. For joining an existing garden, the city page does not describe a process, so ask your community association or the garden itself. The page also points to the Calgary Horticultural Society for more information.

kitchener-cambridge-waterloo.heading: How to find a community garden plot in Kitchener and Waterloo
paragraphs: This describes the City of Waterloo and the City of Kitchener side of the region; Cambridge has its own programs. Waterloo's community gardens page sends people who want to learn about a garden or request a plot to the Waterloo Region Community Garden Network. Kitchener's own garden guidance also directs people looking for a plot to that network.

The City of Waterloo page says each garden is run by a volunteer team of about 3 to 5 people, and the teams are responsible for assigning plots fairly. So sign-up rules and waitlists differ garden by garden. The city's gardens email on that page is listed for people starting a new garden, not for plot requests.

new-york.heading: How to join a community garden in New York City
paragraphs: Many of New York City's community gardens are connected to GreenThumb, a program of NYC Parks, and the gardens are run by volunteer garden groups. GreenThumb offers an online map for finding a garden, and each garden has a GreenThumb community engagement coordinator you can contact while you search.

Joining usually means reaching out to a garden group rather than applying to the city for a plot. NYC Parks has a How to Join page, and it says many gardens keep limited open hours from April 1 to October 31, so check the page for details on hours and sign-up steps.

links.label: NYC Parks GreenThumb: join a garden

san-francisco.heading: How to get a community garden plot in San Francisco
paragraphs: This covers the City and County of San Francisco, where the Recreation and Park Department supports and manages dozens of community gardens. Its community gardens page says you must be a San Francisco resident to be given a plot. You can ask to be placed on the wait list for a specific garden, and when your name reaches the top, you are contacted about a plot.

Waits can be long. A Recreation and Park garden page lists a multi-year wait at Golden Gate Park, and a Potrero Hill garden group says its list may take several years. Check each garden's page for current wait information, and ask whether it offers any way to take part while you wait.

links.label: SF Recreation and Park: community gardens
Potrero Hill Community Garden: how to join

salt-lake-city.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Salt Lake City
paragraphs: Many community gardens in Salt Lake City are run by Wasatch Community Gardens, a nonprofit. To get a plot you join a waitlist by submitting its online garden plot application, and plots are assigned in order of application date. The nonprofit says some fee reductions may be available depending on need and funding.

Gardens are organic, and Wasatch Community Gardens describes a real time commitment: tending your plot, shared service tasks and garden events, plus a spring orientation meeting. Its page does not state a residency rule and does not give deadlines, so check the page for current details because this can change.

links.label: Wasatch Community Gardens: join a community garden

edmonton.heading: How to join or start a community garden in Edmonton
paragraphs: The City of Edmonton says there are over 80 community gardens in the city. The city does not hand out plots itself. Its Community Garden Map shows which gardens accept public members, and you contact each garden group directly to ask about joining.

Waitlists and plot availability vary from garden to garden, so it helps to ask a few. If you want to start a garden on city parkland instead, the city points to its community garden guidelines and suggests calling 311 or emailing communitygardens@edmonton.ca to be connected with a Neighbourhood Resource Coordinator.

hamilton.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Hamilton, Ontario
paragraphs: This describes the City of Hamilton. The city provides space for community gardens in parks and on other city-owned land, and says each garden is managed by a collective of residents or a nonprofit agency. The page lists 22 gardens on city land, and Powell Park is noted as temporarily closed.

There is no single city application for plots. The Hamilton Community Garden Network, run by the Neighbour to Neighbour Centre, keeps a directory of gardens and who to contact. Each garden has its own application process and waitlist, so contact the garden you are interested in.

cleveland.heading: How community gardens work in Cleveland
paragraphs: This describes the City of Cleveland. Many neighborhood gardens take part in Summer Sprout, a program run by the City of Cleveland with Ohio State University Extension. The program supports gardens with seeds, plants and hydrant access, and the program's site has separate Join a Garden and Start a Garden sections.

To start a new Summer Sprout garden, the garden leader first completes the Dig In! training, then submits the program's application. Suburban gardens in Cuyahoga County go through the OSU Extension office instead. Check the program page for current forms and deadlines, since these change each season.

links.label: Summer Sprout: Cleveland's community gardening program

cincinnati.heading: How to find a community garden plot in Cincinnati
paragraphs: The Civic Garden Center of Greater Cincinnati, a nonprofit, keeps a Community Gardens Network Map. You pick the kind of garden you want (allotment gardens have plots used by individual gardeners), find one near you, and contact the garden coordinator listed on the map to ask how to get involved.

Each garden sets its own process, so ask about availability and rules directly. If you want to turn a vacant lot into a garden and it is city-owned, the City of Cincinnati's Office of Environment and Sustainability says to contact it, and it can find out which department controls the parcel and whether it can be leased.

links.label: Civic Garden Center community gardens map

san-diego.heading: Community gardens in San Diego: how the city handles them
paragraphs: This describes the City of San Diego. The city's Parks and Recreation page for community gardens is mainly about starting a garden on city property. It links an application form, petition form, sample contract and a development checklist, plus a map of publicly accessible gardens.

The page does not describe a single citywide waitlist for plots. To join an existing garden, use the map to find one near you, then contact the garden or the park's recreation staff to ask how plots are assigned. Rules and availability differ by garden.

links.label: City of San Diego community gardens

providence.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Providence
paragraphs: Providence gardens fall into a few groups. Southside Community Land Trust, a nonprofit, runs gardens and keeps a waitlist form; it says it gives priority to people who live within one mile of each garden. Other gardens sit on City park land, and those are described as open to anyone in the surrounding community.

For city park gardens, you contact the coordinator listed for that garden, and the Providence Parks Department has a Community Gardener in Residence for general questions. Gardens run by agencies, churches and schools keep their own waitlists. Many gardens have waitlists, so ask early.

links.label: Southside Community Land Trust: community gardens

san-antonio.heading: Community gardens in San Antonio: where to start
paragraphs: San Antonio does not appear to have a single city plot application. The main hub is Green Spaces Alliance of South Texas, a nonprofit whose Urban Land and Water Program supports a network of community gardens and helps communities set up new ones. Gardens inside San Antonio city limits can join its network.

Its site has a map of community gardens with contact details and work day schedules, which is the practical way to find a garden near you and ask the garden directly about joining. The same page covers how to start a garden, including organizing volunteers and leaders and finding partners.

links.label: Green Spaces Alliance: Urban Land and Water Program

columbus.heading: Community gardens in Columbus: the city's Land Bank program
paragraphs: This describes the City of Columbus, Ohio. Its Community Garden Program is run by the Land Bank's Division of Land Redevelopment and covers gardens on Land Bank lots. It is aimed at people who want to start and tend a garden on a vacant parcel, rather than at renting a single plot in an existing garden.

You email the division with the area you have in mind, and if a site is available, staff send an application. It asks for the parcel, your background and goals, a funding plan, a signed liability waiver and a simple site plan. Approved gardeners sign a license agreement that is renewed each year. The city's page lists a license fee and renewal fee, so check the page, this can change. The page does not mention a residency rule or a waitlist.

louisville.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Louisville
paragraphs: In Louisville Metro, the Parks department runs an Urban Agriculture Program that manages community gardens inside Metro Parks. The program's page points people to an interest form that adds them to the community garden plot waitlist, so you ask to be listed rather than choosing a plot directly.

Metro Parks also keeps a separate Growing around Louisville page that lists outside groups offering garden plots. Those groups set their own sign-up rules, so contact the one nearest you. The city pages do not give waitlist times, so ask when you sign up.

links.label: Louisville Metro Parks: Urban Agriculture Program

houston.heading: Community gardens in Houston: the Parks Urban Garden Program
paragraphs: The City of Houston Parks and Recreation Department has an Urban Garden Program that helps community groups turn selected spots in city parks into community gardens, with help from the department's Urban Gardener. It works through groups rather than handing out individual plots, and not every park qualifies. The city's page lists a short set of eligible parks.

Garden groups are responsible for finding their own supplies and for day-to-day upkeep, and the land must be used for gardening or farming only. The page lists an email address for the Urban Gardener, for questions or to get involved with an existing garden, and an online registration link. Nonprofits and other groups also run gardens in the Houston area, and each sets its own sign-up rules.

pittsburgh.heading: How to find or start a community garden in Pittsburgh
paragraphs: Pittsburgh gardens are run by a mix of groups, so there is no single waitlist. Grow Pittsburgh, a nonprofit, keeps a community garden map where each listing has contact details and says whether the garden has open plots. You contact the garden directly to ask about joining.

Some gardens sit on city land and take applications through the City of Pittsburgh's Department of Public Works. One example listed on Grow Pittsburgh's directory uses an online application, a three-year lease and a limit of one plot per household. Fees and terms differ by garden, so check each listing. If you want to start a new garden, Grow Pittsburgh offers New Garden Support and workshops, and its page lists a phone number and email for questions.

sacramento.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Sacramento
paragraphs: This describes the City of Sacramento. Its Department of Youth, Parks and Community Enrichment operates several permanent community gardens, including Bill Bean Jr. Park, Blackbird Park, Fremont and others. The department's page gives a program contact by name, with an email and phone number, for questions about the program and how to rent a plot.

The page lists each garden with its address and approximate number of plots, and it shows a yearly price per plot, so check the page, this can change. It does not describe a waitlist, and it does not state availability for any garden, so ask the contact which gardens have openings. Sacramento County Regional Parks is a separate agency that runs its own garden at Gibson Ranch, with its own sign-up.

buffalo.heading: How to join or start a community garden in Buffalo
paragraphs: In Buffalo, the main network is Grassroots Gardens WNY, a nonprofit that supports community gardens in Buffalo and Niagara Falls. Joining an existing garden is free. You use the garden finder on its site to locate one near you, then contact the organization to get connected.

To start a new garden, you submit the group's community garden application. It asks for a team of at least five committed community members who will look after the garden for five years, a public lot and the landowner's consent. Neighborhoods with limited access to fresh produce are approved first. The page does not list deadlines, so call or use the contact page to ask about the current round.

links.label: Grassroots Gardens WNY: start a garden

tampa-st-petersburg.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Tampa
paragraphs: This describes the City of Tampa's program, not St. Petersburg's or Pinellas County's. The Parking Community Garden is created and run by the city's Parking Division. To apply you must be 18 or older and live inside Tampa city limits (or be a city employee). The city warns that a Tampa mailing address does not guarantee you are inside the city, so check its boundary map.

Plots are not first come, first served. The city runs an application window and then picks gardeners by random lottery, with some plots set aside for people who need ADA access. Only one application per person is allowed. At the time of our last check, applications were closed, so check the page, this can change.

links.label: City of Tampa Parking Community Garden

indianapolis.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Indianapolis
paragraphs: In Indianapolis, Indy Parks and Recreation manages two community gardens with rentable plots: one near Eagle Creek Park (56th Street and Reed Road) and one at 2400 N. Tibbs Ave. The city describes the plots as available to rent for a small fee, so check the page, this can change. For Eagle Creek, the city lists 317-327-7110 as the number to call to reserve a plot.

Registration and plot sizes can change from year to year, so confirm current details with Indy Parks before you plan your season. Neighborhood groups and nonprofits also run their own community gardens around the city, and those have separate sign-up rules.

links.label: City of Indianapolis: community gardens and urban farms

raleigh.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Raleigh
paragraphs: Raleigh Parks runs a community garden program in partnership with the Inter-Faith Food Shuttle and local groups. Two park gardens have individual plots: Barwell Road Park Community Garden and Eastgate Park Community Garden, which has accessible plots. The city also lists raised garden boxes at several parks and neighborhood centers.

The program page does not lay out an application or waitlist, and its form is for volunteering rather than plot sign-up. For plot availability, the page points to the program's email, CommunityGardens@raleighnc.gov, and phone, 919-996-2767.

atlanta.heading: Starting or joining a community garden in Atlanta
paragraphs: The City of Atlanta's main garden program, AgLanta Grows-A-Lot, is about starting a new garden or farm rather than renting a plot. It lets residents, nonprofits and entrepreneurs apply for a renewable five-year license to use vacant city-owned land. The first step is an online site inquiry form for a property on the program's map.

If none of the listed properties fits, the city's page suggests joining an existing garden or farm instead. Those gardens are run by neighborhood groups and nonprofits, each with its own sign-up rules. Questions about Grows-A-Lot go to the Mayor's Office of Resilience.

jacksonville.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Jacksonville
paragraphs: One city-linked option is the Riverside Community Garden in Willow Branch Park, run by Jacksonville Parks and Recreation together with the nonprofit Riverside Avondale Preservation. It has 31 raised plots, and the garden asks members to volunteer a set number of hours each quarter. Plots are assigned to city residents at the start of each year, and first-time gardeners are offered half plots.

The garden has said it is at capacity, and openings go to people on its waitlist, with waits of several months to a year. Check the page for current status and fees, this can change. The UF/IFAS Duval County Urban Gardening Program also rents plots at its Superior Street garden to county residents and can answer questions about other gardens.

oklahoma-city.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Oklahoma City
paragraphs: This describes a county program, not a City of Oklahoma City one. The Oklahoma County Community Health Department runs a community garden at its Northeast Regional Health and Wellness Campus, 2600 NE 63rd St. Its membership form says members must live in Oklahoma City or Oklahoma County, be interested in sustainable agriculture, and take part in an approved volunteer activity.

On the form you choose between a standard raised bed and a limited number of ADA-approved plots. The form lists a community garden monitor as the contact for questions. Fees and season details were not clear to us, so check the form, this can change.

links.label: Oklahoma County Health Department garden membership form (PDF)

memphis.heading: How to get a community garden plot near Memphis
paragraphs: The main public option is run by Shelby County, not the City of Memphis. Shelby County Community Gardens, at Gardener Road, assigns plots by season to Shelby County residents who apply online. Check the page for current fees and rules, this can change.

Plots have filled before the season starts. The county's site has said new applications were closed once plots were taken and suggested checking back in early March for the next season. The site also has a separate renewal page for returning gardeners.

richmond.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Richmond
paragraphs: In the City of Richmond, community gardens fall under the Richmond Grows Gardens program, which sits in the city's Parks and Recreation department. The city does not hand out individual plots. Each garden group decides how its own plots are assigned, so you contact the garden you want to join. The program's Our Gardens page lists them.

The city's page has said many established gardens are looking for gardeners, and that the program is not taking applications for brand-new community gardens. If a garden has a waitlist, the program coordinator may be able to point you to another site. The page does not spell out residency rules, so ask the garden or the coordinator. Check the page, this can change.

hartford.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Hartford
paragraphs: Most community gardens in the City of Hartford are run by KNOX, a Hartford nonprofit. Its site describes 21 community gardens with room for more than 300 families. New gardeners apply through an online form on the KNOX community gardens page, and returning gardeners get a renewal application by mail at the start of each year.

The KNOX page has said the new-gardener form opens in January, that applicants are contacted when plots open up, and that gardeners pay a small seasonal fee. It does not list the amount, how the waitlist works or any residency rule. Check the page, this can change, or call KNOX at the number it lists.

orlando.heading: How to get a community garden plot in Orlando
paragraphs: The City of Orlando lists its community gardens on a Green Works page, but there is no single citywide plot application. The page says each garden is managed by its own group, which sets its own bylaws and keeps its own waiting list.

To get a plot, pick a garden near you from the city's list and contact it directly, then ask about its waitlist and what it needs from new members. The page gives contact emails for most gardens, and for a couple of city-supported sites it lists the city's Green Works email instead. It does not say how to start a new garden.

virginia-beach-norfolk.heading: Community garden land in Norfolk (Hampton Roads)
paragraphs: Hampton Roads has several city governments, so this section covers only the City of Norfolk, not Virginia Beach. Norfolk's Grow Norfolk program is for groups that want to manage a garden on a whole city-owned parcel, not for individuals asking for a single plot. A nonprofit or business has to act as sponsor, sign an agreement with the city and carry liability insurance.

The application page asks for at least five households or businesses committed to the garden, with those within a mile of the site identified, plus a letter of support from the local civic league. At the time of our last check the page said no lots were available. Check the page, this can change, or contact the Grow Norfolk coordinator listed there.

new-orleans.heading: Getting garden land in New Orleans
paragraphs: The City of New Orleans does not run a plot-rental program listed on its site. Its urban agriculture work is based in the City Planning Commission, where an Urban Agriculture Liaison focuses on helping growers get land. The city's page says it plans to work with the New Orleans Redevelopment Authority (NORA) to make that process clearer.

NORA's annual property auction has included properties that farmers and gardeners can bid on, and the city links a guide to the auction for growers. For trouble with a city process such as permitting or water meters, the page points to the urban agriculture email address it lists. To join an existing garden instead, contact that garden directly.
